title: Classes, constructors and static members
body: A class is a blueprint for objects: it declares fields (stored data), methods (behaviour) and constructors (initialization). `new Account("Ada")` allocates an object on the heap, runs the matching constructor and returns a reference. Members are private by default; mark the members other code needs as `public`.

A constructor has the class's name and no return type. Constructors can chain with `: this(...)` to avoid duplicating setup. If a class declares no constructor, the compiler supplies a public parameterless one; once you declare any constructor, that default disappears. Object initializers (`new Account("Ada") { Limit = 50 }`) set accessible properties after the constructor runs.

Primary constructors (C# 12) put parameters on the type declaration: `class Account(string owner)`. The parameters are in scope throughout the class body. If a member uses one, the compiler captures it in a hidden field; it is not a property and stays mutable inside the class. Assign it to a `readonly` field or property when you want an explicit, immutable member.

`static` members belong to the type, not to an instance: `Account.Count` is shared by all accounts. A static constructor runs once before the type is first used. A `static class` contains only static members and cannot be instantiated; it is the home for helpers and, as you will see later, extension members.

`this` refers to the current instance and disambiguates a field from a parameter of the same name. Before adding state, check whether it belongs to each object (instance) or to the type (static), and whether a constructor leaves every field in a valid state.
challenge: Rewrite a Temperature class with a primary constructor (double celsius), a readonly Celsius property initialized from it, a computed Fahrenheit property and a static FromFahrenheit factory. Print 100 C in F and 212 F in C.
question: What happens to the compiler-supplied parameterless constructor once a class declares its own constructor?
wrong: It is still generated alongside yours
reasoning: The implicit default constructor exists only when you declare none, so `new Account()` stops compiling once you add Account(string).
